body:
Paul travels to Jerusalem and presents the Gospel he has been preaching to the Gentiles to the leaders of the Church. Although Paul believes his mission has come from God, he does not separate himself from the Church. His mission is recognized alongside Peter’s: Peter is called primarily to the Jews, while Paul is called to the Gentiles. Different missions, but one Gospel.

Later, however, Paul confronts Peter in Antioch. Peter had been freely eating with Gentile Christians, demonstrating that through Christ they belonged fully to the same community. But when certain Jewish Christians arrived, Peter withdrew from the Gentiles out of fear of what others might think. His actions began communicating something contrary to the Gospel he already knew to be true, and others followed his example.

The conflict reveals something deeply human. Peter had not stopped believing the truth; fear caused him to stop living consistently with it.

Paul’s response also reveals an important balance within Christian life. He respects the authority and unity of the Church, yet he is willing to speak when someone’s actions contradict the Gospel—even when that person is Peter.

This reading therefore asks more than What do I believe? It asks something harder:

Where might my actions contradict a truth about Christ that I already know?
theme: The Gospel is not only something we believe; it is something we are called to live consistently, even when doing so costs us the approval of others.
prayer: Lord Jesus, You know the truths I profess and the places where I struggle to live them. Give me the courage to remain faithful when fear, approval, or the opinions of others pull me away from You. Help me recognize when my actions contradict what You have already taught my heart. Give me humility when I need correction, courage when I need to stand firm, and grace to live the Gospel I profess. Amen.
opening: Peter knew the truth. He had even been living it. Then something changed.
title: Should we really care about what other people think?
